prompt: Coreto's Checkout team has six engineers, a sprint of ten working days and six focus hours a day per engineer. What is its capacity in a sprint, in hours?
Júlia calls the 90-hour group-bookings request "a corner of one sprint". By the lesson, what does the sum R$ 13,500 leave out?
hint: Where would the 90 hours come from?

choices.text: The festival's ticket fees, which would pay for the feature several times over
choices.why: That is the benefit side, and it was already in the room. The missing piece is on the cost side.

choices.text: The work those hours were already planned for
choices.why: Right: the team has no idle hours, so the 90 come out of the strategy's own work, and that delay is part of the price.

choices.text: The overhead of meetings around the feature
choices.why: Meetings are already outside the six focus hours a day; the estimate is in focus hours.

choices.text: A margin for the estimate being wrong
choices.why: A margin would make the number larger, and it would still price the feature as though the hours were free.

prompt: Saying yes to group bookings pushes the lock removal back by one sprint. Using lesson 5's price for the seat-hold debt, what does that sprint add to the cost of the yes?
hint: Interest is charged per sprint while the debt stays.

choices.text: R$ 48,000, the principal of the debt
choices.why: The principal is what fixing the debt costs; delaying the fix does not add it again.

choices.text: R$ 13,500, the same as the feature
choices.why: That is the feature's own 90 hours. The delay has a separate price.

choices.text: 31 h of interest, R$ 4,650
choices.why: Right: every team touching the module pays 31 hours a sprint for as long as the debt stays, so one more sprint of debt costs that.

choices.text: Nothing, as long as the lock removal still ends this year
choices.why: Interest is paid every sprint the debt exists, whatever year the fix lands in.

prompt: The lesson says the group-bookings request "collides twice" with Coreto's strategy. Which are the two collisions? Choose all that apply.
hint: One is about people, one is about code.

choices.text: It takes hours from the work the strategy put first
choices.why: Yes: the 90 hours come out of Checkout's move onto the new hold interface.

choices.text: It adds new holds to the path the policy protects
choices.why: Yes: group holds are changes to the reservation path, which takes nothing without load-test evidence.

choices.text: It was asked for by product instead of by engineering
choices.why: Who asks is not a collision; a request from engineering that crossed the policy would collide the same way.

choices.text: It serves one client instead of all venues
choices.why: Serving one client is a product judgement. The strategy says nothing about it.

prompt: Box Office asks Checkout for 90 hours to add a waiting room in front of checkout on on-sale mornings. By the lesson, what should Mateus answer?
hint: Does it compete with the guiding policy, or serve it?

choices.text: No, for the same 25% reason as group bookings
choices.why: The hours are the same, and the strategy is the test, not the hours: this request protects the on-sale.

choices.text: Not yet, until the lock removal is finished in August
choices.why: A waiting room protects the on-sale while the locks are still there, which is when it is worth most.

choices.text: Yes, even if other work has to move
choices.why: Right: a request that serves the guiding policy gets a yes even when it is inconvenient.

choices.text: Ask Box Office to take the request to Helena
choices.why: Escalation is for a request that competes with the strategy. This one agrees with it.

prompt: Match each part of a no to what a strategy supplies for it.

pairs.right: The guiding policy and the action the request would delay
Something that serves the need and stays inside the policy
A date or condition from the strategy's own plan

right_distractors: How busy the team is this sprint

prompt: Mateus considers offering "a simpler version of group holds" as his alternative. Why does the lesson reject it?

choices.text: It would take longer than the full feature
choices.why: A simpler version would be quicker. The objection is where it lands, not how long it takes.

choices.text: It still adds holds to the protected path
choices.why: Right: an alternative that crosses the policy is the same request, smaller, and meets the same objection.

choices.text: The festival would refuse anything less than the full feature
choices.why: Nobody asked the festival. The lesson rejects it on the strategy's terms.

choices.text: An alternative has to come from another team
choices.why: The Box Office route happens to involve another team; that is not what makes an alternative good.

prompt: Why does Mateus's reply say plainly that a group cannot pick its own seats on the map?
hint: What happens when an oversold alternative is found out?

choices.text: To make the alternative look worse, so Júlia accepts the date
choices.why: That would be a manipulation; the reason given is trust in the next alternative.

choices.text: Because Box Office asked him to
choices.why: Box Office plays no part in the wording. The honesty is Mateus's own choice.

choices.text: The terms of the festival's contract require it
choices.why: The lesson says nothing about a contract. The reason is about the relationship with the asker.

choices.text: The asker finds out anyway, and trust suffers
choices.why: Right: a good alternative is honest about what it gives up, or the next one is not believed.

prompt: A lead refuses a request with "the team is busy". By the lesson, what does a reason citing the guiding policy change?
hint: Where does the argument go next?

choices.text: The argument moves on to whether the strategy is right
choices.why: Right: a disagreement with the policy belongs with Helena, who owns it, instead of with the lead's calendar.

choices.text: It ends the discussion, because the policy is final
choices.why: The policy is not final: the asker may disagree with it, and that disagreement goes to the strategy's owner.

choices.text: It makes the no sound less personal, which is its main value
choices.why: It does sound less personal, but the lesson's point is where the next argument happens.

choices.text: It lets the lead skip the alternative and the date
choices.why: The reason is one of three parts; citing the policy does not replace the other two.

prompt: The lock removal runs two quarters from 1 March, so the date in Mateus's reply is the first Checkout sprint of ___.
Match each vague condition to the checkable one the lesson puts beside it.

pairs.right: When the load test passes an on-sale replay with group holds
After the lock removal, planned to end in August
When every Checkout call to the hold path uses the new interface

right_distractors: When the team feels the path is stable

prompt: Why does the lesson call "later" the dangerous answer?

choices.text: The asker hears a yes with no date and plans around it
choices.why: Right: it feels kind, and it is a no delivered months late, after the asker has spent credibility on it.

choices.text: It commits the team to building the feature
choices.why: It commits the team to nothing, which is the problem: a not-yet with a condition is the answer that commits.

choices.text: It is ruder than a plain no
choices.why: It sounds gentler than a no. The danger is what it promises, not its tone.

choices.text: Product teams are trained to escalate it
choices.why: A no is what gets escalated. "Later" gets believed, which is worse.

prompt: A team asks to start extracting a service from coreto-core this year. What answer does the lesson give, and why?

choices.text: Not yet, until the lock removal finishes
choices.why: The end of the lock removal does not lift this one; the migration waits a year by decision.

choices.text: Later, so the team stays motivated
choices.why: "Later" is the answer the lesson warns against, whatever the motive.

choices.text: Yes, provided it stays off the reservation path
choices.why: The cloud-cost project got that condition. The migration was ruled out for the year.

choices.text: A plain no, citing the page
choices.why: Right: it is on the page's list of things the company will not do, and no condition this year would change that short of changing the strategy.

prompt: A load test cannot promise the day it will pass. What does the lesson say to give instead of a date for the condition?
hint: A commitment the team keeps whatever the result.

choices.text: A range of dates with a confidence level
choices.why: That is a forecast of the result. The lesson asks for something the team controls.

choices.text: No date, so as not to overpromise
choices.why: A not-yet with no date to look again decays into a later.

choices.text: The end of the year, as a safe outer bound
choices.why: A distant bound with nobody checking is a later with a date on it.

choices.text: The date on which a named person will check it
choices.why: Right: a review date puts the question back in front of somebody on a known day, whatever the test shows.

prompt: In September the load test passes with group holds. The team then says the condition is now a second load test in December. By the lesson, what has happened?
hint: A condition that moves each time it is met.

choices.text: Ordinary caution: a second test lowers the risk
choices.why: Each move has a plausible reason; that is exactly how the disguise passes.

choices.text: The strategy changed, so the condition had to
choices.why: Nothing says the strategy changed. If it had, the honest move is to say so and re-answer.

choices.text: A disguised no that nobody was willing to say
choices.why: Right: a receding condition is a no the asker cannot escalate, and it costs belief in every later condition.

choices.text: The review date did its job
choices.why: The review produced a new condition instead of the yes the old one promised.

prompt: Davi's not-yet table shows three requests in one quarter all waiting on the same load-test condition. What does the lesson say that is?

choices.text: A sign that the condition is too vague to check
choices.why: The load-test condition is checkable; several requests waiting on it says something about its cost.

choices.text: A reason to turn the three into plain noes
choices.why: The condition is still honest; nothing in the pattern makes the requests impossible.

choices.text: Evidence for the next review of the strategy
choices.why: Right: a condition blocking several requests costs the business something, and the strategy review is where that cost is weighed.

choices.text: Proof that the Reservations team is too small
choices.why: It is evidence to weigh, and team size is one possible answer among several.

prompt: A 90-hour request lands on a team with 360 hours in a sprint. What share of the sprint does it take, in percent?
Put the paragraphs of Mateus's written reply in the order he wrote them.
hint: The decision comes first and the escalation last.
items: The no, with the policy as its reason
Who decides if the festival cannot wait
trap: Leading with the cost buries the decision: the reader has to reach the third paragraph to learn the answer is no.

prompt: Mobile asks Platform for 40 hours to build a new analytics dashboard, far from the reservation path. Platform's sprint is fully planned for the on-sale load test. What is the honest answer?
hint: A request collides in either way alone.

choices.text: Not yet, with a date and the hours it costs
choices.why: Right: it collides on capacity alone, so the answer carries the cost to the strategy's work and a date tied to that work.

choices.text: Yes, because it does not touch the protected path
choices.why: Staying off the path avoids one collision; the hours still come out of the load test the strategy put first.

choices.text: A plain no, citing the guiding policy
choices.why: A dashboard is not on the not-list and does not cross the policy; once the load test is done, the objection goes away.

choices.text: Later, since 40 hours is small
choices.why: Small requests add up, and "later" promises nothing the asker can plan with.

prompt: Four requests of 90 hours each add up to one whole ___ of the Checkout team.
